section: 1 Introduction
citing_passage: External generalization is already a substantive concern in RAC prediction. Jadhav et al. reported deterioration when models were transferred between compiled RAC datasets despite favourable within-dataset results [10]. Grouped validation has also been used to examine heterogeneity in high-performance concrete [11]. More generally, validation should reflect the dependence structure and intended prediction setting, and leakage control extends beyond separating row identifiers [12,13]. Blocking related observations can itself create a harder extrapolation task, so a source-disjoint score must be interpreted with its deployment target rather than treated as an automatically unbiased universal estimate.

section: 2.1 Data and strength-label scope
citing_passage: The main dataset was version 1 of the Mendeley Data release identified by DOI 10.17632/3xvfyycp8d.1 [9]. We used all 1,736 original compressive-strength records. The compiler supplied an outlier flag based on Isolation Forest, with strength among the numerical inputs used for flagging. We did not use this target-informed flag to remove records or as a predictor. Retaining the original records avoids conditioning the reliability assessment on a prior outcome-based screen. The slump database was checked for availability in the earlier study stage but was not modelled here.

section: 2.3 Frozen cross-source evaluation and point predictor
citing_passage: The point predictor was the fixed ExtraTreesRegressor implementation of extremely randomized trees [30], with 200 trees, minimum leaf size 3, all eleven features available at each split, one execution thread and fixed run-specific seeds. No hyperparameter search was conducted for this study phase. The scale model described below had the same tree count and feature fraction, with minimum leaf size 10. All models, auxiliary fits, splits and predictions originated in the frozen experimental stage. The manuscript and figures introduce no additional model fitting.

section: 2.4 Calibration and interval-cost comparisons
citing_passage: For adaptive intervals, a separate scale predictor learned log(1 + |e_OOF|) from three-fold component-disjoint out-of-fold errors within the fitting partition. Calibration and test labels were excluded from this scale training. The predicted scale was σ(x) = max[1, exp(g(x)) − 1] MPa. Source-balanced calibration was then applied to rᵢ/σ(xᵢ), yielding radius q_A σ(x). This is residual-scale adaptation, not conformalized quantile regression [15]. A group-maximum comparator calibrated on the maximum absolute residual within each calibration component. Its aim differs from ordinary marginal coverage, so its row coverage is presented as a conservative cost reference rather than a like-for-like optimal method.

section: 4.1 Coverage gains must be assessed with interval cost
citing_passage: Source balancing changes which calibration records influence the residual distribution. Giving each publication equal total weight prevents a large source from determining the calibration target simply through its record count.
